procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated March 09, 2017 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad in Criminal Misc. Bail Application No. 4652 of 2017, granting bail to respondent No. 2.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Respondent No. 2 filed a bail application before the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad (Criminal Misc. Bail Application No. 4652 of 2017). The High Court allowed the bail application vide order dated March 09, 2017, granting bail to respondent No. 2.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court was approached in two appeals: 1) A Criminal Appeal arising out of Special Leave Petition (Crl.) No. 5611 of 2017, filed by the appellant, on whose complaint the case against respondent No. 2 was registered. 2) An appeal preferred by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), both challenging the High Court's order granting bail to respondent No. 2.

issue.issue_text: whether there is any prima facie or reasonable ground to believe that the accused had committed the offence;

facts: The accused was alleged to have committed the heinous crime of killing an old lady by strangulation.
A neighbour saw the accused coming out of the victim's house around the time the alleged murder occurred.
law: When considering a bail application, a court must evaluate whether there is a prima facie or reasonable ground to believe that the accused committed the offense.
For serious offenses, a court granting bail must provide reasons for its prima facie conclusion.
application: The Supreme Court noted that the High Court had completely lost sight of the basic principles for granting bail.

The Court found that the neighbour's testimony of seeing the accused leave the victim's house around the time of the incident gave rise to a reasonable belief that the accused had committed the murder.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that there was a reasonable ground to believe the accused had committed the murder. Based on this prima facie case and the heinous nature of the crime, the Court determined that bail should not have been granted, especially since charges had not yet been framed.

arguments.issue_text: whether there is any prima facie or reasonable ground to believe that the accused had committed the offence;
appellant_arguments: The appellant, who is the complainant, relied on reports from expert bodies, including the AIIMS Medical Board, to argue that there was a prima facie case against the accused regarding the cause of death, and therefore, the High Court should not have granted bail.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (the accused) argued that the expert reports were not final or conclusive.
He contended that the reports were based on a postmortem of photographs of the deceased, not the actual body, and therefore should not be given much credence.
He pointed out that the AIIMS Medical Board itself had cautioned that its opinion on the cause of death needed to be corroborated with circumstantial evidence.
He argued that the High Court had rightly exercised its discretion in granting bail, and that such a discretionary order should not be interfered with unless it is shown to be perverse.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Having regard to the limited scope of interference with an order granting bail and keeping in mind the parameters on which such an order can be interdicted, the reasons given by the High Court to grant bail to the respondent cannot be termed as perverse. The High Court kept in mind the relevant factors, and therefore, the Supreme Court will not interfere with the discretionary order.
legal_tests_applied: The primary test for interfering with a High Court's order granting bail is whether the order is 'perverse' or suffers from the 'vice of non-application of mind'.

Factors to be borne in mind while considering an application for bail are: (i) whether there is any prima facie or reasonable ground to believe that the accused had committed the offence; (ii) nature and gravity of the accusation; (iv) danger of the accused absconding or fleeing, if released on bail; (vii) reasonable apprehension of the witnesses being influenced; and (viii) danger, of course, of justice being thwarted by grant of bail.

While an elaborate examination of evidence should be avoided at the bail stage, there is a need to indicate in such order reasons for prima facie concluding why bail was being granted, particularly where the accused is charged with a serious offence.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant failed to demonstrate that the High Court's order granting bail was perverse.
The Supreme Court's scope of interference with a discretionary order like granting bail is limited, and the appellant did not provide sufficient grounds to warrant such interference.
why_respondent_won: The High Court's order granting bail is a discretionary one, and the Supreme Court will not normally interfere unless it is shown to be illegal or perverse.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court had exercised its discretion judiciously and had provided reasons for its decision, which could not be termed as perverse.
policy_considerations: Personal liberty is a very precious fundamental right and it should be curtailed only when it becomes imperative according to the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case.
There is a necessity to introspect whether denying bail to an accused person is the right thing to do on the facts and in the circumstances of a case.
It is imperative for High Courts to sensitise judicial officers to properly comprehend the importance of personal liberty vis-à-vis social interests and to maintain a fine balance between them.
